root.note: One Chinese character, said in different ways: tê in Hokkien (Min Nan), chá in Mandarin and Cantonese. Words like tea come from the first, words like chai from the second.

stages.meaning: a hot drink made with leaves and water

history: Chinese has one written sign for tea, 茶, but it is said in different ways. In Hokkien, spoken around the port of Xiamen, it is tê. Dutch traders bought tea there in the 1600s, and their word thee went into English, French (thé) and German (Tee). In many other places the word came from chá, the form in Mandarin and Cantonese: Portuguese chá, Russian чай, Hindi chai, Turkish çay. Roughly: where the Dutch brought tea by sea, people say something like ‘tea’; where tea came over land, or through the Portuguese in Macau, they say something like ‘cha’. In the 1700s many English people still said tea like ‘tay’. And British slang has both: a cup of tea is also a cup of char.
historyEinfach: Tea comes from Chinese. In one Chinese language, tea is tê. Dutch traders brought tea and the word to northern Europe. Then English said tea. In other Chinese languages, tea is chá. This word went to Russia, India and Turkey. In Hindi, tea is chai. English has this word too: chai is tea with milk and spices.

synonyms.note: UK, informal: a cup of tea

elsewhere.text: Hindi chāy comes from the other Chinese form, chá. English borrowed this word too, much later: chai is spiced tea with milk. So English has the same Chinese word twice, by two different roads.
Russia got its tea over land, by caravans through Mongolia and Siberia, so Russian has the chá word, not the tê word.
